lesson.title: Ping: Is Anybody Home?
lesson.summary: Ping is a diagnostic utility that sends an ICMP echo request to a destination and waits for an ICMP echo reply, using the round trip to test reachability and measure latency.
lesson.body:
The simplest question you can ask about a remote machine is whether it is there at all and how long it takes to hear back from it. Ping answers that question directly, and it does so using two of the ICMP message types introduced in the previous chapter: echo request, type 8, and echo reply, type 0.

When you run ping against an address, your machine builds an ICMP echo request packet, stamps it with an identifier and a sequence number, attaches a small block of data, and sends it toward the destination. If a host is listening at that address and its network stack is willing to answer, it copies the identifier, sequence number, and data straight back into an ICMP echo reply and sends that reply to the original sender. Nothing about this exchange involves an application, a listening service, or a port number. Echo request and reply are handled directly by the network stack itself, which is exactly why ping works as a test of basic IP reachability rather than a test of any particular service.

Consider pinging a public DNS resolver at 8.8.8.8. Your machine sends an echo request carrying sequence number 1. Roughly twenty milliseconds later, an echo reply arrives carrying the same sequence number and the same data you sent. Ping reports that round trip time, then sends sequence number 2, then 3, and so on, building up a small picture of both latency and reliability. If reply 4 never comes back, ping reports it as lost, and a run with several losses out of many requests tells you something is dropping packets somewhere on the path, even before you know where.

Two limits are worth keeping in mind. First, a successful ping only proves that IP connectivity and ICMP handling work between the two endpoints, not that a specific application on the destination is running or reachable, since a web server can be down while the underlying host still answers pings. Second, many firewalls and routers are configured to silently drop or rate limit ICMP echo traffic as a security measure, so a host that does not answer ping is not necessarily unreachable or offline, it may simply be choosing not to respond. Ping is a fast first check, not a definitive one, and the next chapter builds on the same ICMP foundation to answer a different question: not just whether a destination is reachable, but which routers the packets pass through on the way there.
